definition: Widespread or common in a particular place or at a particular time.
example: Thick morning fog is prevalent along this stretch of coast in early summer.
nuance: Prevalent means found widely; predominant means strongest or most numerous among rivals, so a thing can be prevalent without leading.
prompt: A biologist surveys which plants grow in a large meadow.
options: Clover was prevalent across the meadow, covering nearly every patch of ground.
Clover was prevalent in the meadow, though she found only one sprig all day.
Her field notes were prevalent to the study because she knew the meadow well.
The clover was so prevalent that each stem stood a meter taller than the grass.
reasons: A plant found almost everywhere in the area is widespread there.
A single sprig after a full day of searching means the plant is scarce.
This confuses the word with relevant; it describes how common something is, not whether it matters.
Height has nothing to do with how widely something occurs.

practice.prompt: A teacher grading sixty essays keeps seeing the same spelling mistake.
options: The mistake was prevalent, appearing in just one essay out of sixty.
She called the error prevalent because it changed one sentence's meaning so badly.
The students prevalent the error by checking each other's drafts.
Mixing up its and it's was prevalent in the essays, showing up in almost every one.
reasons: One case out of sixty makes the error rare, the reverse of widespread.
How serious a single mistake is says nothing about how often it occurs.
The word is an adjective, not a verb; this seems to confuse it with prevent.
An error that turns up in nearly all the papers is common throughout the group.
